outputs.L3:
An audio signal processing apparatus is configured to receive and process an audio signal that contains audio data for one or more audio objects associated with a three-dimensional image. Each audio object may correspond to a visual object or element within the three-dimensional image, such that the perceived position of the sound can be coordinated with the perceived position of the visual content.

The audio signal includes depth position data for the audio object. This depth position data indicates a target depth position, which represents where the audio object is intended to be perceived in three-dimensional space. For example, the target depth position may specify whether the audio object should appear in front of, at, or behind a display plane.

The apparatus includes a determiner that identifies a visual rendering depth range of a target three-dimensional display. The visual rendering depth range defines the range of depths that the display is capable of presenting to a viewer. Different three-dimensional displays may have different depth capabilities, and therefore the same target depth position may need to be adapted depending on the particular display being used.

A mapper is provided to convert the target depth position of the audio object into a rendering depth position based on the visual rendering depth range of the target three-dimensional display. In this way, the audio object can be positioned in a manner that is compatible with the depth characteristics of the display. The conversion may involve scaling, shifting, clipping, or otherwise transforming the target depth position so that it falls within the display’s available rendering depth range.

The mapper may further adjust the sound source positions of audio objects so that they align with the depth positions of corresponding visual objects shown by the three-dimensional display. As a result, the perceived location of each audio object can be made consistent with the perceived location of its associated visual object. This alignment improves the coherence of the audiovisual presentation and enhances the viewer’s sense of immersion in the three-dimensional scene.
outputs.L4:
An audio signal processing apparatus is configured to process object-based audio content associated with a three-dimensional image. The object-based audio includes a plurality of audio objects, and each audio object is provided with position information indicating where the corresponding sound source is intended to be perceived in a three-dimensional space. In particular, the position information includes depth position data that is linked to, or corresponds with, depth information of one or more visual objects in the three-dimensional image.

The apparatus receives information defining a visual depth range of a target three-dimensional display. This visual depth range represents the range of depths within which the display can accurately present visual objects to a viewer. Since different 3D displays may have different depth reproduction capabilities, an intended depth position contained in the original audio-visual content may not always coincide with a depth that can be faithfully rendered by the target display.

To address this, the apparatus maps the target depth position of each audio object to a rendering depth suitable for the target display. The mapping is performed on the basis of the display’s visual depth range, so that the perceived position of each sound source is adjusted to correspond to the depth at which the associated visual object is actually rendered. For example, if a visual object originally has a depth outside the accurately renderable range of the display, the visual depth may be compressed or shifted into the available display depth range. The associated audio object is then similarly mapped so that its rendered sound position remains aligned with the displayed visual object.

After determining the appropriate rendering depth for each audio object, the apparatus generates audio rendering information or processed audio signals for reproduction by a loudspeaker system, headphone system, or other spatial audio output device. The resulting audio output causes the listener to perceive each audio object at a spatial position that is consistent with the corresponding visual object as presented on the target 3D display.

By adapting audio object depth positions according to the actual visual depth capabilities of the display, the apparatus improves consistency between sound localization and three-dimensional imagery. This reduces perceptual mismatch between audio and video, enhances immersion, and provides a more natural audio-visual experience across different types of 3D display devices.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps us point to something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we may mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book that the listener or reader can identify.

The word “the” gives clarity and precision to sentences. It helps connect ideas and makes meaning more exact. Without it, English would often sound incomplete or unclear. Phrases such as “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future” show how this simple word can refer to things that are unique, familiar, or already known.

Although “the” is short and easy to overlook, it is one of the most frequently used words in English. It reminds us that even the smallest words can have great importance in language.

The apparatus receives audio object data including at least one depth position associated with an audio object in a three-dimensional audio scene and obtains display depth range information indicative of a visual rendering depth range supported by the target three-dimensional display. A depth mapping unit maps the depth position of the audio object from an audio scene depth range to the visual rendering depth range of the display to generate a mapped depth position. A spatial audio rendering unit renders the audio object using the mapped depth position to produce one or more output audio signals having spatial characteristics corresponding to the visual depth presentation. The apparatus thereby aligns perceived audio object depth with the depth range available for visual rendering on the target display, improving audiovisual correspondence for three-dimensional content.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention involving a receiver, determiner, and mapper for aligning audio object positions with corresponding visual objects in a three-dimensional image.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention is an audio-visual alignment system for three-dimensional media. It is designed to make the perceived positions of audio objects match the positions of corresponding visual objects shown in a 3D image or scene.

The system includes three main functional components:

1. **Receiver**  
   The receiver obtains:
   - audio object information, such as one or more sound sources or audio objects;
   - position information for those audio objects, for example coordinates, direction, distance, or spatial metadata; and
   - three-dimensional image information containing visual objects that correspond to the audio objects.

2. **Determiner**  
   The determiner analyzes the 3D image information and determines the positions of the relevant visual objects in the three-dimensional image space. It may identify where a person, vehicle, instrument, speaker, or other visual element appears in the 3D scene. The determiner can compare the visual object positions with the associated audio object positions to detect misalignment between what is seen and what is heard.

3. **Mapper**  
   The mapper maps or transforms the position of each audio object so that it corresponds to the position of its associated visual object in the 3D image. This may involve adjusting the audio object’s spatial metadata, such as azimuth, elevation, depth, distance, or 3D coordinates. The mapped audio object position is then used for rendering spatial audio so that the sound is perceived as coming from the same location as the visual object.

In operation, the receiver receives audio and 3D visual data, the determiner determines the location of a visual object corresponding to an audio object, and the mapper modifies or associates the audio object’s position with that visual object’s position. As a result, when the content is reproduced on a display and sound system, the viewer hears the audio object from a location that aligns with the visual object in the three-dimensional image.

This invention is useful for immersive media such as 3D films, virtual reality, augmented reality, gaming, telepresence, and spatial audio/video playback, where accurate correspondence between visual and auditory cues improves realism and reduces perceptual inconsistency.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2
